added_claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
added_claims.quote: And Trump says, and I hope he has a plan, that it's all going to be better on the other side of this, but uh obviously the stock markets are getting nervous.
added_claims.claim: American exceptionalism has been dented because the hegemon is disrupting its own system, and equity markets are nervous because there may be no plan behind the promise that things will be better after the disruption.

added_claims.direction: US equities weaker on policy uncertainty
added_claims.testable: partly - equity returns versus policy uncertainty index

added_claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
added_claims.quote: he knows politics better than I do, and he thinks 80% of Americans love terrorists
added_claims.claim: Tariffs are politically popular with the American public (the caption's 'terrorists' is 'tariffs'; even his well-educated mother liked them), so economists' objections have little political traction and tariffs are less likely to be dropped.

added_claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
added_claims.quote: there's not a lot of open water between really the left where the left was in the US and Trump
added_claims.claim: Protectionism is bipartisan in the US (Bernie Sanders ran on similar trade positions in 2016), so tariffs are not a one-person quirk and are more likely to persist after the current administration.

added_claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
added_claims.quote: You don't have one election in France or Germany suddenly changing everything. Change a lot but not everything.
added_claims.claim: Europe's institutional stability (single elections change a lot but not everything) makes it a more stable geopolitical counterweight to a US whose direction can reverse with each presidential election.

added_claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
added_claims.quote: we saw it under Biden where the Republicans thought inflation was way higher than it was and the Democrats thought inflation was way lower than it was
added_claims.claim: Partisan bias in perceived inflation is symmetric: under Biden Republicans overstated inflation and Democrats understated it, so survey-based sentiment and inflation expectations are contaminated by party identity.
added_claims.indicator: survey inflation expectations by party (University of Michigan type surveys)
added_claims.testable: yes - survey expectations split by party

added_claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
added_claims.quote: I'm making a political economy call I'm not saying there's some, you know, constellation of shocks that's just going to happen in a certain way and create inflation
added_claims.claim: His inflation forecast is a regime-level political-economy call (central banks will not stand firm when a shock arrives), not a point forecast of a specific shock sequence; he does not claim to know the trigger or the date.
added_claims.direction: higher inflation in the next shock

added_claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
added_claims.quote: I think we're going to see him reach into the toolkit. And you know, Fed independence comes later.
added_claims.claim: Sequence of political responses to inflation: first the executive reaches for tools such as price controls and financial repression, and only later does a direct fight over Fed independence arrive.
added_claims.indicator: price controls, financial repression measures, Fed independence
added_claims.conditions: inflation returning under a president averse to higher rates

added_claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
added_claims.quote: there are people who lose by having interest rates high
added_claims.claim: Even with strong jobs, high interest rates have losers (young people buying houses and cars), which creates political pressure on the Fed and makes a showdown likely when it hikes against inflation.

added_claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
added_claims.quote: If you want to give people more stuff and bigger transfers, all for it, more power to you, but raise taxes.
added_claims.claim: Concern about debt is not the same as support for austerity: bigger transfers are fine if financed by taxes, but treating deficit spending as a free lunch is the error.

added_claims.speaker: Kenneth Rogoff
added_claims.quote: It would be so stupid because we we can print money. We don't need to default on our Treasury bonds.
added_claims.claim: A US default or forced restructuring of Treasuries is not a realistic scenario because the US issues its own currency and can inflate or repress instead, so the risk is inflation or higher yields, not default.
added_claims.conditions: sovereign issuing its own major currency

added_claims.quote: we put in all these restrictions to make the bank safer that had them basically hold more Fed debt, which is basically Treasury bonds and more
added_claims.claim: Post-crisis bank safety rules already forced banks to hold more Treasuries, a form of financial repression that creates captive demand for government debt and can be extended further.

corrections.issue: Conflates two points. Rogoff says the Draghi report made the point that Europe has lagged in tech and should be more independent; the link that military spending often funds early-stage tech is Rogoff's own comment, not the Draghi report's.
corrections.fix: Rogoff: Draghi's report argued Europe has lagged in tech and needs more tech independence; he adds that defence and tech are connected because military spending often supplies early funding for tech start-ups.

completeness_estimate: 0.90 - first reader captured nearly all of the macro arguments (tariffs, dollar, China, inflation outlook, central bank independence, debt); missed some political-economy supports (tariff popularity, bipartisan protectionism), sequencing remarks, the default and bank-regulation points, and a few host-quoted theses.
